title: Attraction
subtitle: Drag the king onto the fork square — then collect.
goals: Sacrifice to relocate the enemy king
Chain two tactics into one combination

steps.say: A fork only works when both targets stand on forkable squares — so what if they don't? ATTRACTION: sacrifice a piece to DRAG a target onto the right square. The most common version in all of chess: Bxf7+ pulls the king onto f7, where a knight check will fork him with whatever else is loose. Look at Black's queen on c6 — it's loose, and f7 is one knight-check away from it.

steps.prompt: Black's queen sits loose on c6. Drag the king onto the forking square and win her!
hints: From e5, your knight would check a king on f7 AND attack c6. So put the king on f7 — by force.
Bxf7+! The king must deal with it — then Ne5+ forks king and queen.

line.say: The attraction sacrifice — the bishop dies to relocate the king onto the fork square...
And there it is: check from e5, and the same knight attacks the c6 queen. The king must step away...
The queen falls. Even after ...bxc6 recaptures the knight, count it: bishop and knight for queen and pawn — a winning trade everywhere on earth. Attraction turned a 'safe' queen into a fork victim.

rejections.say: The fork square without the fork — Black's queen simply steps aside, and your knight achieved nothing. The KING must stand on f7 first: Bxf7+ drags him there by force.
It attacks the queen, she moves, life goes on. Attraction thinking asks a better question: which SACRIFICE puts a royal target on my knight's forking square?

steps.wrongSay: The knight fork exists only if the king stands on f7. What forces him there?
steps.successSay: Sacrifice to relocate, then fork — two cheap tactics chained into one queen-winning combination.

steps.prompt: Now the most famous attraction move ever played. Levitsky–Marshall, Breslau 1912 — Black to move. Legend says the spectators showered the board with gold coins afterward. Find Marshall's move!
hints: Marshall put his queen on the ONE square where all three captures lose instantly: two pawn captures open mating nets, and the queen capture walks into a royal fork.
Qg3!! — into the heart of White's pawns. Check each capture: hxg3 allows ...Ne2#, fxg3 allows ...Ne2+ and ...Rxf1#, and Qxg3 meets ...Ne2+ forking king and queen.

line.say: THE gold-coin move. The queen attacks h2, stands en prise three ways — and every capture loses: hxg3 Ne2# (smothered by his own pawns), fxg3 Ne2+ then Rxf1#, and Qxg3 Ne2+! forking king and queen. White resigned on the spot. The d4 knight was the silent partner: every line runs through its e2 fork.

rejections.say: The fork without the setup — Kh1! and the knight must retreat with nothing to show. Marshall's genius was the ORDER: the queen goes to g3 first, and only then does e2 become unanswerable.
Kxh2 — a rook for a pawn. The immortal move puts the QUEEN on g3, where taking her in any of three ways loses on the spot.

steps.wrongSay: The move is a queen move — onto a square defended three times. Trust the knight on d4.
steps.successSay: Qg3!! — many call it the most beautiful move ever played. You found it from the same chair Marshall did.
